title: God Has Spoken in His Son
summary: God, who spoke in many ways through the prophets, has now spoken finally through his Son, the heir of all things, the radiance of his glory, who made purification for sins and sat down at God's right hand. A chain of seven Old Testament quotations then shows that the Son is far greater than the angels: they worship and serve, while he reigns forever as Son, God, Creator, and King.
story: Hebrews begins where the Old Testament leaves off. For centuries God spoke to Israel through prophets, at many times and in many ways, and every word was true but partial. Now, in what the author calls "these last days", God has spoken through a Son. The first chapter sets out who that Son is, because everything that follows depends on it: the warnings, the priesthood, the new covenant, the call to endure. The comparison with angels may seem strange to a modern reader, but it was the natural place to begin. In Jewish tradition angels had mediated the law at Sinai (2:2; see also Acts 7:53 and Galatians 3:19), and they stood at the top of the created order. To show that the Son is above them is to show that the message he brings outranks even the law.
historical:
The date and audience of Hebrews are uncertain (see the introduction), but the readers were almost certainly steeped in the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, which the author quotes throughout. Jewish thought in this period gave angels a large place. Texts from the Dead Sea Scrolls and other Jewish writings of the time speak of angelic priests in a heavenly temple, archangels who lead God's armies, and angels who carry prayers and revelations. Colossians 2:18 warns against the worship of angels, so some Christians were clearly tempted to give them too much honor.

The opening verses also echo the language Hellenistic Jewish writers used for divine Wisdom. The Wisdom of Solomon, a Jewish book written in Greek probably in Alexandria in the century or so before Christ, calls Wisdom a reflection of eternal light and an image of God's goodness. Hebrews applies similar language to a person, the Son, and adds what no Jewish writer had said of Wisdom: that he made purification for sins and sat down at God's right hand.
cultural:
Sitting at a king's right hand meant sharing his authority and honor. In the ancient Near East, a victorious king might put his feet on the necks of defeated enemies, and a footstool carved with images of enemies expressed the same idea; Psalm 110:1, quoted in verse 13, draws on that picture. The quotations in verses 5-13 come largely from royal psalms, songs originally used at the coronation or wedding of Israel's kings, where the king was called God's son (Psalm 2:7, 2 Samuel 7:14). Early Christians read these psalms as pointing beyond any king of David's line to the Messiah, and Psalm 110 became one of the Old Testament texts most often quoted or echoed in the New Testament.

The word firstborn in verse 6 carries the idea of rank and inheritance, not only birth order. In Psalm 89:27 God promises to make David's heir his firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth. Heir, in verse 2, carries the same sense: the Son receives the whole estate.
literary: Verses 1-4 are one long, carefully constructed sentence in Greek, rich in sound and rhythm, and among the finest prose in the New Testament. It opens with alliteration (many times, many ways, fathers, prophets all begin with p in Greek) and moves from God's past speech to the Son's identity, work, enthronement, and superiority. The rest of the chapter is a chain of seven quotations (a form sometimes called a catena): Psalm 2:7 and 2 Samuel 7:14 (verse 5), a line found in the Greek text of Deuteronomy 32:43 and similar to Psalm 97:7 (verse 6), Psalm 104:4 (verse 7), Psalm 45:6-7 (verses 8-9), Psalm 102:25-27 (verses 10-12), and Psalm 110:1 (verse 13). They are arranged in contrasts: to the Son God says you are my Son; about the angels he says they are winds and flames. The chain begins and ends with a rhetorical question, "to which of the angels did God ever say" (verses 5 and 13), and closes with the answer in verse 14: angels are servants of those who will inherit salvation.

outline.t: God's final word in the Son
The Son, whom the angels worship
Angels as servants, the Son as eternal King
The Son enthroned; the angels sent to serve

doctrines.note: God has spoken, first through the prophets and finally through his Son. The Son does not merely bring a message from God; he is God's self-expression, "the exact representation of His nature" (verse 3). Earlier revelation was true but partial; in the Son it reaches its fulfillment.

The Son is distinguished from God the Father and yet shares his glory, creates the universe, upholds all things, is addressed as God (verse 8), and is called Lord and Creator (verse 10). The church's later confession of the Son as fully God and eternally distinct from the Father is built in large part on passages like this.
The royal psalms, promises made to David's line, are fulfilled in Jesus, who is the Son, the anointed King, and the one seated at God's right hand.

Tucked into the middle of the opening sentence is the whole message of the book: "After He had provided purification for sins, He sat down." The priestly work is complete, and the seated posture says so.

words.note: Apaugasma, radiance or brightness. It can mean light shining out from a source or light reflected back. Either way, the Son is to God's glory what brightness is to the sun: not a second light but the same light shining. Early theologians, such as those at Nicaea in AD 325, found the image useful because light and its radiance are never separated in time.

Charakter, the impression made by a stamp or seal, like the image on a coin that exactly matches the die. The Son is the exact imprint of God's nature (hypostasis, being or essence). The word says that to see the Son is to see what God is.

Katharismos, cleansing or purification, a word from the world of worship and ritual purity. It anticipates the argument of chapters 9 and 10, where the author shows that Christ's blood cleanses the conscience in a way that animal sacrifices could not.

Prototokos, firstborn. Here it is a title of rank and inheritance more than of birth, echoing Psalm 89:27, where God makes David's heir his firstborn. It does not imply that the Son was created; the same chapter calls him the Creator (verse 10).

christ: This is one of the New Testament's highest descriptions of Christ. He is heir of all things, agent of creation, the radiance of God's glory and exact representation of his being, the one who upholds the universe by his word, the priest who made purification for sins, and the King seated at God's right hand. Hebrews applies to him Psalm 45's address, "Your throne, O God, endures forever and ever", and Psalm 102's words about the Lord who laid the foundations of the earth and remains unchanged when the heavens wear out. Yet the chapter speaks of him as the one through whom God speaks "in these last days", a person in history, and the next chapter insists that he became fully human. The Christian confession of one Lord, truly God and truly man, begins to take shape here.

hard.q: Psalm 45 and Psalm 102 seem to be about an Israelite king and about God. How can Hebrews apply them to Jesus?
hard.a:
Psalm 45 is a royal wedding song, and in its original setting it praised a king of David's line, addressing him in exalted language that includes the Hebrew word elohim, God. Interpreters take that address in different ways: as a courtly title for a king who represents God, or as language that already strained beyond any ordinary king and so was read by later Jews and Christians as messianic. Psalm 102 is the prayer of an afflicted person addressed to the LORD, and verses 25-27 praise God as the unchanging Creator.

Hebrews does not claim that the original singers had Jesus consciously in view. It reads these psalms as parts of one story whose fulfillment has now appeared. If Jesus is the promised Son of David, the royal psalms find their true king in him; and if the Son is the one through whom God made the universe (verse 2), then words addressed to the Creator are rightly addressed to him. The early church followed the same practice elsewhere, applying to Jesus Old Testament texts about the LORD (Philippians 2:10-11 takes up Isaiah 45:23). Readers who find this method strained often find it less so once they grant the author's starting point: that the Son is divine.

questions: The chapter says God has spoken finally in his Son. What difference does it make that God's clearest word is a person and not only a set of teachings?
Verse 3 says the Son upholds all things by his powerful word. How might that change the way you think about ordinary things that seem to run on their own?
Angels are described as servants sent for the sake of those who will inherit salvation. What does that suggest about how much God cares for his people?
